'''Roger Brent''' (born December 28, 1955) is an American biologist known for his work on gene regulation and [[systems biology]].  He studies the quantitative behaviors of cell signaling systems and the origins and consequences of variation in them. He is full member in the Division of Basic Sciences at the [[Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center]] and an affiliate professor of Genome Sciences at the [[University of Washington]].

==Early life==
Brent grew up in [[Hattiesburg, Mississippi]], and received his BA in Computer Science and Statistics from the [[University of Southern Mississippi]], where he applied AI techniques to protein folding.  He performed PhD (1982)<ref>"Regulation of the cellular response to DNA damage" (1982)</ref> and postdoctoral work (1985) in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology at [[Harvard University]] in the laboratory of [[Mark Ptashne]].  In work there he cloned the [[Repressor lexA|E. coli LexA repressor]] and showed how it controlled the cell's response to DNA damage, used LexA as a repressor in yeast,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Brent|first1=Roger|last2=Ptashne|first2=Mark|title=A bacterial repressor protein or a yeast transcriptional terminator can block upstream activation of a yeast gene|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|date=1984|volume=312|issue=5995|pages=612–615|bibcode=1984Natur.312..612B|doi=10.1038/312612a0|pmid=6390216|s2cid=4309764}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=North|first1=G.|title=Latterday lessons of lambda and lac.|journal=Nature|date=1984|volume=308 | issue = 5961|pages=687–688|pmid=6232462|doi=10.1038/308687a0|s2cid=4240047|doi-access=free}}</ref> and created fusion proteins that used LexA to bring portions of yeast Gal4 and other transcription regulatory proteins to synthetic reporter genes in yeast.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Brent|first1=Roger|last2=Ptashne|first2=Mark|title=A eukaryotic transcriptional activator bearing the DNA specificity of a prokaryotic repressor|journal=[[Cell (journal)|Cell]]|date=1985|volume=43|issue=3|pages=729–736|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(85)90246-6|pmid=3907859|doi-access=free}}</ref>  These domain swap experiments established the domain structure of eukaryotic transcription regulatory proteins.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Alberts|first1=A.|last2=Bray|first2=D.|last3=Lewis|first3=J.|last4=Raff|first4=M.|last5=Roberts|first5=K.|title=Molecular Biology of The Cell|date=1989|publisher=Garland Science |chapter=Membrane Structure |isbn=978-0-8153-4432-2|at=p. 568: Figure 10–24 |edition=6th}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Frankel|first1=A. D.|last2=Kim|first2=P. S.|title=Modular Structure of Transcription Factors: Implications for Gene Regulation|journal=Cell|date=1991|volume=65|issue=5|pages=717–719|pmid=2040012|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(91)90378-c|s2cid=6632853}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Genetics: Lecture 21|url=https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/34953/7-03Fall-2001/NR/rdonlyres/Biology/7-03GeneticsFall2001/36E8F9BF-ECCE-4872-AA02-609A6C9257A8/0/fa01lec21.pdf|hdl=1721.1/34953|website=[[MIT OpenCourseWare]]|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|access-date=December 15, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200518044628/https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/34953/7-03Fall-2001/NR/rdonlyres/Biology/7-03GeneticsFall2001/36E8F9BF-ECCE-4872-AA02-609A6C9257A8/0/fa01lec21.pdf|archive-date=May 18, 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Grotewold|first1=E.|last2=Kellogg|first2=E.|last3=Chappell|first3=L|title=Plant Genes, Genomes and Genetics|date=June 2015|publisher=John Wiley and Sons|isbn=978-1-119-99887-7|edition=1st}}</ref>

==Career==

Brent's use of [[prokaryote|prokaryotic]] repressor proteins in [[eukaryote]]s, and development of [[fusion protein|chimeric protein]]s containing prokaryotic DNA binding domains, enabled identification of other transcription regulatory domains<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Godowski|first1=P. J.|last2=Picard|first2=D.|last3=Yamamoto|first3=K. R.|title=Signal transduction and transcriptional regulation by glucocorticoid receptor-LexA fusion proteins |journal=Science |date=August 1988|volume=241 | issue = 4867 |pages=812–816|pmid=3043662 |doi=10.1126/science.3043662|bibcode=1988Sci...241..812G}}</ref> and gene regulatory technologies including tetracycline-repressor controlled transcriptional repression<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Deuschle|first1=U.|last2=Meyer|first2=W. K.|last3=Thiesen|first3=H. J.|title=Tetracycline-reversible silencing of eukaryotic promoters|journal=Molecular Cell Biology | date=April 1995 |volume=15 | issue = 4 |pages=1907–1914|pmid=7891684 |doi=10.1128/mcb.15.4.1907|pmc=230416}}</ref> and the Gal4 and LexA UAS systems used in other model organisms.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rodriguez|first1=A. D. V|last2=Didaniol|first2=D.|last3=Desplan|first3=C.|title=Power tools for gene expression and clonal analysis in Drosophila|journal=Nature Methods |date=2012|volume=9|issue=1|pages=47–55|pmid=22205518|doi=10.1038/nmeth.1800|pmc=3574576}}</ref>  The use of DNA binding domains to target tethered functional protein domains (for example double strand endonucleases <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bibikova|first1=M. J.|last2=Carroll|first2=D.|last3=Segal|first3=D. J.|last4=Trautman|first4=J.K.|last5=Smith|first5=J.|last6=Kim|first6=Y. G.|last7= Chandrasegaran|first7=S.| title= Stimulation of homologous recombination through targeted cleavage by chimeric nucleases. |journal= Mol Cell Biol |date=January 2001|volume=21 |issue=1|pages=289–297|pmid= 11113203 |doi= 10.1128/MCB.21.1.289-297.2001 |pmc=88802}}</ref> and DNA methylases <ref>{{cite journal|last1=van Steensel|first1=B.|last2=Henikoff|first2=S.| title= Identification of in vivo DNA targets of chromatin proteins using tethered dam methyltransferase |journal= Nat. Biotechnol. |date=April 2000|volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=424–428|pmid= 10748524 |doi=10.1038/74487|s2cid=30350384}}</ref>) or bait moieties in two-hybrid experiments to defined sites on DNA is now routine.

In 1985, Brent moved to the Department of Molecular Biology at [[Massachusetts General Hospital]] and the Department of Genetics at [[Harvard Medical School]].  His work there contributed to two-hybrid methods and to development of large scale/ general purpose [[functional genomics|functional genomic]] means (interaction mating <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Finley, Jr|first1=R. L. Jr.|last2= and Brent|first2=R. |title=Interaction mating reveals binary and ternary interactions between Drosophila cell cycle regulators|journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA|date=1994|volume=91|issue=26|pages=12980–12984|pmid=7809159|doi=10.1073/pnas.91.26.12980|pmc=45564|doi-access=free}}</ref> and development of peptide [[aptamer]]s) to detect and disrupt protein-protein interactions.<ref name="US Patent">{{cite web|last1=Brent|first1=Roger|last2=Ptashne|first2=Mark|title=Regulation of eukaryotic gene expression US Patent 4,833,080 (1989)|url=http://www.uspto.gov/|access-date=January 6, 2015}}</ref> In 1997, with [[Sydney Brenner]] he helped establish the Molecular Sciences Institute,<ref>{{cite book|last1=Friedberg|first1=Errol|title=Sydney Brenner: A Biography|date=October 2010|publisher=[[CSHL Press]]|isbn=978-0-87969-947-5}}</ref> a nonprofit research laboratory in [[Berkeley, California]], and became its CEO,<ref>{{cite web| title=Proteomics: Current State and Future Directions - An interview with Roger Brent, PhD |url=http://www.chidb.com/newsarticles/issue70.ASP|access-date=July 5, 2010}}</ref> research director and president in 2001.  He initiated his lab's studies on cell signal control and cell-to-cell variation there. He is now a Professor of Basic Sciences at the [[Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center]] and an Affiliate Professor of Genome Sciences and Bioengineering at the [[University of Washington]].

Brent's work pursues two main questions: how cell signaling systems control their signals and the information those transmit <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Yu|first1=R.|last2=Gordon|first2=A.|last3=Colman-Lerner|first3=A.|last4=Benjamin|first4=K. R.|last5=Pincus|first5=D.|last6=Serra|first6=E.|last7=Holl|first7=M.|last8=Brent|first8=R.|title=Negative feedback optimizes information transmission in a cell signaling system|journal=Nature|date=2008|volume=456|issue=7223|pages=755–761|doi=10.1038/nature07513|pmc=2716709|pmid=19079053}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Brent|first1=R|title=What is the signal and what information does it carry?|journal=[[FEBS Letters]]|date=2009|volume=583|issue=24|pages=4019–24|pmid=19917282|doi=10.1016/j.febslet.2009.11.029|s2cid=15873809}}</ref> and the origins and phenotypic consequences of cell-to-cell variation in signaling and subsequent responses.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Colman-Lerner|first1=A.|last2=Gordon|first2=A.|last3=Serra|first3=E.|last4=Holl|first4=E.|last5=Brent|first5=R.|title=Regulated cell-to-cell variation in a cell fate decision system|journal=Nature|date=2005|volume=437|issue=7059|pages=699–706|doi=10.1038/nature03998|pmid=16170311|bibcode=2005Natur.437..699C|s2cid=4398874}}</ref>

In 1987, Brent helped found, and continues to contribute to, ''Current Protocols in Molecular Biology'', a "how to clone it manual"<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ausubel|first1=F. M.|last2=Brent|first2=R.|last3=Kingston|first3=R. E.|last4=Moore|first4=D. D.|last5=Seidman|first5=J. G.|last6=Smith|first6=J. A.|last7=Struhl|first7=K|section=Preface|title=[[Current Protocols in Molecular Biology]]|date=2012|volume=98 |pages=iii–v|doi=10.1002/0471142727.mbprefs98|isbn=978-0-471-14272-0|s2cid=221604713|doi-access=free}}</ref> which started the ''[[Current Protocols]]'' journals. From 1995 to 2000 he organized the "After the Genome" workshops in Santa Fe, whose content contributed to some of the early systems biology agenda.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Gruber|first1=M|title=Map the Genome, Hack the Genome|url=http://archive.wired.com/wired/archive/5.10/genome.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140913013038/http://archive.wired.com/wired/archive/5.10/genome.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 13, 2014|website=[[Wired.com]]|access-date=2 February 2010}}</ref> In addition to customary advisory work with NIH, NSF, and industrial organizations, in 1997 he began to advise the US government on tactical and strategic considerations for defense against biological attack and emerging diseases.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Marshall|first1=E.|title=Too radical for NIH? Try DARPA |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |date=1997 |volume=275|issue=5301|pages=744–746|doi=10.1126/science.275.5301.744|pmid=9036531|s2cid=5825319}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Miller|first1=J.|last2=Broad|first2=W. J.|last3=Engelberg|first3=S.|title=Germs: Biological Weapons and America's Secret War|date=2001|publisher=Simon and Schuster|location=New York|isbn=978-0-684-87159-2|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/germsbiologicalw00mill_0}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bhattacharjee|first1=Y.| title=Panel Provides Peer Review of Intelligence Research |journal=Science|date=2007|volume=318|issue=5856|page=1538|doi=10.1126/science.318.5856.1538|pmid=18063763|s2cid=41060126|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite report |type=Draft |last1=Brent|first1=R.|title=In the valley of the shadow of death |website=DSpace@MIT |hdl=1721.1/34914|date=2006-11-22}}</ref>  In 1998, at the Molecular Sciences Institute, he participated in discussions with Rob Carlson and Drew Endy that helped develop some of the ideas underpinning [[synthetic biology]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Carlson|first1=R|title=BIO-IO Components and Design Tools|url=http://www.synthesis.cc/BIO-IO.pdf|access-date=5 August 2010|display-authors=etal}}</ref> From 2011 to 2014 he directed the Center for Biological Futures, an experimental effort to better understand the impacts of advances in biological knowledge and capability on human affairs.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Woodward|first1=Kristin|title=Center for biological futures to address challenges posed by explosion of biological knowledge in 21st century|url=http://www.fredhutch.org/en/news/releases/2011/10/center_for_biological_futures.html|website=Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center|publisher=[[Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center]]|access-date=6 January 2014|date=2011-10-13}}</ref>

He has been a scholar of [[The Pew Charitable Trusts]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Pew Scholars Program in the Bio-Medical Sciences|url=http://www.pewtrusts.org/en/projects/pew-biomedical-scholars/directory-of-pew-scholars/1987/roger-brent|website=The PEW Charitable Trusts |access-date=10 October 2011}}</ref> and a senior scholar of the [[Ellison Medical Foundation]].<ref>{{cite web|title=HOME::Senior Scholar Award in Aging::2000::Stem Cells|url=http://www.ellisonfoundation.org/content/identification-protein-regulators-self-renewal-differentiation-and-senescence-embryonic-stem|website=The Ellison Medical Foundation|publisher=[[Ellison Medical Foundation|The Ellison Medical Foundation]]|access-date=8 August 2011}}</ref> In 2003 he shared the Gabbay Award in Biotechnology and Medicine for his work on protein interaction methods,<ref>{{cite web|title=PAST WINNERS 2003 "for their development of yeast two-hybrid and yeast mating interaction traps"|url=http://www.brandeis.edu/rosenstiel/gabbayaward/past.html|website=Rosenstiel Basic Medical Sciences Research Center|publisher=Brandeis University Rosenstiel Basic Medical Sciences Research Center|access-date=13 June 2012}}</ref> and in 2011 he was named a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] "for outstanding contributions in the area of biochemistry, transcription, genomics, and systems biology."<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Sausville|first1=E. A.|title=Awards, Appointments, Announcements|journal=[[J Natl Cancer Inst]]|date=2011|volume=103|issue=4|page=295|doi=10.1093/jnci/djr038|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Brent's use of prokaryotic repressor proteins and chimeric proteins to regulate gene expression in eukaryotes was the subject of basic patents (including {{US patent|4833080}}, Regulation of Eukaryotic Gene Expression, with Mark Ptashne). Dr. Brent is the inventor on 16 additional US patents and four pending US patents.<ref>{{cite web|title=Patent search at USPTO.gov|url=http://patft.uspto.gov|access-date=December 20, 2022}}</ref>

==Personal==
In 2006, Brent married biologist and 2004 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine laureate [[Linda B. Buck]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SRD2K80JYpYC&pg=PA180 |title=Nobel Faces |last=Badge |first=Peter |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |page=180 |year=2008 |access-date=December 2, 2015|isbn=978-3-527-40678-4 }}</ref>
